post.description: Assess knowledge base health: coverage, freshness, and readiness for AI consumption. Send exactly one of articles (mode A) or url (mode B); an empty body is a 400. Mode A: up to 300 articles and a 2 MB request body. Only title and content are required per article; other fields on an article are ignored. Mode B: reads a public help centre server-side (Zendesk Help Center API first, then sitemap.xml), up to 300 articles and 10 MB, about 50 seconds at most. It honours robots.txt, never follows a redirect to another host, and refuses private, loopback and metadata addresses. Limits: 5 URL reads per hour per IP and 3 per help centre domain per hour; if the limiter is unavailable URL mode returns 503 and articles mode still works. Staleness is computed relative to the time of the request. The result is trimmed for agents: per issue type, a count plus the first 20 examples (index, title, url, reason) in the order the web tool lists them. Article bodies are never returned, and inputs echoes article_count (or the normalised url) instead of the articles.

directions.label: Human Name
directions.description: A recognizable human first name. Creates personal connection but carries the risk of implying the AI is a real person.

directions.label: Human-ish Name
directions.description: A name that sounds like it could be a person but is distinctive enough to signal it might not be. Balances personality with honesty.

directions.label: Brand Extension
directions.description: The company brand name combined with a descriptor. Maximizes brand recognition and is transparent about the AI's role.

directions.label: Character Name
directions.description: A creative, non-human name with personality. Clearly signals 'not a person' while still being memorable and engaging.

directions.label: No Name
directions.description: A functional label describing what the tool does. Maximum clarity and zero pretense, but misses the opportunity for brand personality.

naming.rationale: Regulated environment demands caution. Human names risk implying a licensed advisor is responding. Brand extensions are safest -- they maintain trust while being transparent. No-name (e.g., 'Account Support') is also strong because it avoids personification entirely. Character and human-ish names can work if clearly paired with AI disclosure.

suggestions.rationale: Positions the AI as a knowledgeable guide, aligning with financial advisory expectations.

suggestions.rationale: Clear and functional, avoids any implication of regulated financial advice.

suggestions.name: Acme Bank AI
suggestions.rationale: Maximum transparency, signals technology without making service promises.

suggestions.rationale: Implies intelligent assistance, works for banks promoting AI-powered insights.

disclosure.regulatoryContext: Heavily regulated. CFPB guidance requires transparency in automated financial interactions. Multiple state laws mandate AI disclosure for 'high-risk' interactions including financial services. SEC and FINRA have issued guidance on AI in client communications. California ADMT rules (effective Jan 2027) will require pre-use notice for AI making financial decisions.
disclosure.trustImpact: Financial services customers rank trust as their #1 priority. Upfront AI disclosure, when combined with clear capability scoping, actually reduces anxiety by setting expectations. The key is pairing disclosure with reassurance about security and human oversight.
disclosure.statistic: Only 12% of consumers prefer AI chatbots over humans for financial support, the lowest preference of any industry. However, satisfaction scores improve 22% when AI agents clearly disclose their nature upfront versus being discovered mid-conversation.
disclosure.statisticSource: Katana Consumer Preference Survey 2025; MIT Sloan Management Review AI Disclosure Study

I can help with account inquiries, transaction history, and general guidance. For investment advice or complex account changes, I'll connect you with a licensed advisor.' Always clarify what the AI cannot do (regulated financial advice) alongside what it can.

worryWall.intro: Your team leads will field these questions from their agents. Knowing them helps you craft leadership messaging that cascades down cleanly.

questions.response: No. Be direct. Say the word. 'I know some of you are thinking: does this mean job cuts? Let me be direct: no. Here's why...'
questions.framingGuidance: Even curious teams harbour this fear quietly. Address it early and unprompted to build trust before anyone has to ask.

questions.question: What changes in my day-to-day?
questions.response: Be specific. 'The AI handles [types of tickets]. You handle [types of tickets]. Here's a sample of each.'
questions.framingGuidance: Concrete examples beat abstract promises. Pull real ticket examples from your queue so people can see themselves in the explanation.

questions.question: What if the AI gives wrong answers?
questions.response: Acknowledge it. 'It will make mistakes: just like a new hire on day one. The difference is, it learns faster and you're in control of what it learns.'
questions.framingGuidance: Admitting imperfection is more credible than claiming perfection. Position the team as the safety net, not the bottleneck.

questions.question: Does this mean layoffs?
questions.response: Address head-on. 'Our goal is to handle [X] more tickets without burning out the team. We need more capacity, not fewer people.'
questions.framingGuidance: Nervous teams need you to say the scary word out loud so they know you are not avoiding it. Then reframe around growth.

questions.question: Will I have to train my replacement?
questions.response: Reframe: 'You're the expert. The AI can only be as good as what you teach it. You're not training a replacement: you're building a tool.'
questions.framingGuidance: This fear is really about agency. Emphasise that their expertise is the input, not the output being replaced.

questions.question: Who decided this?
questions.response: Be transparent. 'I did, with input from [leaders]. Here's why, and here's how your voice shapes what comes next.'
questions.framingGuidance: Resistant teams often feel things were done to them. Naming the decision-maker and inviting input restores agency.

questions.question: What if I don't want to work with AI?
questions.response: Empathise, then redirect. 'That's a fair feeling. Let me show you what it actually looks like: not what you're imagining: and then let's talk.'
questions.framingGuidance: Resistance is often rooted in imagined worst-cases. A live demo is worth a thousand reassurances.

Hello Team

We're introducing AI to scale our support capacity without proportionally scaling headcount so that meet growing demand without compromising quality.

I want to share what this means for you.

We're introducing an AI teammate to handle straightforward, repetitive tickets: things like password resets, order status checks, and simple FAQs. This means faster responses for customers and more bandwidth for you to focus on the complex, high-value work.

I know there's scepticism, and I respect that. You've earned the right to be cautious. Here's what I can tell you directly: no headcount changes are tied to this. The AI handles straightforward tickets so you can focus on the complex work only you can do. I'm asking you to watch it in action before forming a final opinion.

Week 3-4: Team reviews AI performance data and provides feedback

We've put together an FAQ covering the most common questions. I'd encourage you to read through it, and please come to me directly with anything that isn't covered.

Best regards

[Leader Name]

meetingScript.title: Start with the business context
meetingScript.copy:
Open with why, not what. 'Our ticket volume is up 30% year-over-year. We've been asking the team to absorb that growth, and it's not sustainable. That's why we're introducing AI: not to replace anyone, but to handle the repetitive work so you can focus on the complex problems only you can solve.'

Framing guidance: Lead with a number the team already feels in their bones. When they nod at the problem, they're primed to hear the solution.

meetingScript.title: Address the fear directly
meetingScript.copy:
Don't wait for someone to ask: they won't, and the silence will fester. Open with: 'I know there's scepticism in this room, and I respect that. You've earned the right to push back.' Then be specific: 'Here's what I decided, here's why, and here's what you control in this process.'

Framing guidance: Resistant teams have often been burned before. Acknowledge that directly. Don't oversell: present facts, name the risks honestly, and give people a real feedback mechanism, not a suggestion box.

meetingScript.title: Demo a real example
meetingScript.copy:
Show, don't tell. Pull up a real ticket from your queue: the kind the AI will handle. Walk through it live: 'Here's a password reset ticket from yesterday. Watch what happens when the AI processes it.' Then show the human review step: 'And here's where you stay in control.'

Framing guidance: Abstract promises create anxiety. A 60-second live demo does more than 20 minutes of slides. Pick a ticket type everyone recognises as tedious.

meetingScript.title: Budget 40% for questions
meetingScript.copy:
Budget at least 40%: maybe more: for questions. With a resistant room, consider making it 50%. Say: 'I expect hard questions and I want them. If I don't have an answer, I'll say so and come back to you within 48 hours.' Have a visible way to capture questions (whiteboard, shared doc) so nothing gets lost.

Framing guidance: Resistant teams need to see their concerns taken seriously in real time. Write questions down visibly. Follow up on every single one. The follow-through after this meeting matters more than the meeting itself.

faq.question: Am I being replaced?
faq.answer: No. We're introducing AI to handle the repetitive, high-volume tickets: password resets, order status checks, simple FAQs. Your role is shifting toward the complex, high-value work that requires human judgement, empathy, and creativity. We need more capacity, not fewer people.

faq.question: What changes in my day-to-day?
faq.answer: In the first few weeks, very little. You'll see a new column showing AI-drafted responses for certain ticket types, and we'll ask you to review them. Over time, the AI takes on more routine tickets, which means your queue shifts toward the interesting, complex problems. We'll provide training and support for every change.

faq.question: Does this mean layoffs?
faq.answer: No headcount changes are tied to this initiative. Our ticket volume is growing faster than we can hire, and this is about adding capacity to the team: not reducing it. If that ever changes, you'll hear it from leadership directly, not discover it through a tool rollout.

faq.question: What if the AI gives wrong answers?
faq.answer: It will make mistakes: just like a new hire on day one. The difference is that every AI response goes through quality checks and human review during the pilot. You are the safety net. If you spot an error, flag it and the AI learns from the correction. We have automatic pause triggers if quality drops below our threshold.

faq.question: Who decided this?
faq.answer: This decision was made by [Leader Name] with input from [leadership team]. We evaluated several options and chose this approach because [brief rationale]. Your voice shapes how this rolls out: the pilot timeline, the ticket types, and the expansion pace are all informed by your feedback.

post.description: Map the compounding feedback loops that make AI support get better over time. Through the API: the compounding graph for a starting automation rate, plus the explainer content (stages, root causes, failure patterns, ticket scenarios) as JSON. buildStages.label: DRAFT
buildStages.detail: You write the workflow. The prompt, the logic, the tools it can use. This is where you define what the AI knows and what it's allowed to do.

buildStages.label: TEST
buildStages.detail: You throw scenarios at it. Does it handle the happy path? What about the weird edge cases? Every failure here is a failure you caught before it reached a customer.

buildStages.label: OBSERVE
buildStages.detail: You watch it handle real conversations. Not metrics yet: just reading the transcripts. Does it sound right? Does it get the nuance?

buildStages.label: REFINE
buildStages.detail: You adjust. Sharpen the prompt. Add a missing tool. Cover that edge case you spotted in observation. The AI gets a little smarter each time.

buildStages.label: LAUNCH
buildStages.detail: It goes live. Real customers, real tickets. But you know now: this isn't the finish line. It's the starting line for the flywheel.

diagnosticCategories.name: Workflow Gap
diagnosticCategories.description: The AI doesn't have a defined process for this type of request.

diagnosticCategories.monitoringSignal: Tickets escalated with "no matching workflow" or where the AI says "I can't help with that."

diagnosticCategories.name: Knowledge Base Gap
diagnosticCategories.description: The AI has the workflow but lacks the specific information needed to resolve correctly.
diagnosticCategories.example: AI quotes an expired return policy because the KB article wasn't updated after a policy change.
diagnosticCategories.fixPattern: Update or create the relevant KB article with current, accurate information.
diagnosticCategories.monitoringSignal: Tickets where the AI gives outdated or incorrect factual information.

diagnosticCategories.name: Prompt Issue
diagnosticCategories.description: The workflow logic or prompt instructions produce incorrect behaviour for this scenario.
diagnosticCategories.example: AI offers a generic apology for a hotel complaint instead of a concrete resolution.
diagnosticCategories.fixPattern: Refine the prompt: add conditional logic, sharpen instructions, add guardrails.
diagnosticCategories.monitoringSignal: Tickets where the AI follows a workflow but produces an inadequate response.

diagnosticCategories.name: Style/Tone Miss
diagnosticCategories.description: The AI resolved the issue but the tone, style, or empathy level was wrong for the situation.
diagnosticCategories.example: AI explains an insurance claim process correctly but sounds clinical when the customer is distressed.
diagnosticCategories.fixPattern: Adjust empathy parameters, add tone instructions for sensitive topics.
diagnosticCategories.monitoringSignal: Resolved tickets with low CSAT or customer comments about the tone.

diagnosticCategories.name: Concept Confusion
diagnosticCategories.description: The AI conflates two similar but distinct concepts, leading to wrong actions.
diagnosticCategories.example: AI treats "reschedule appointment" as "cancel appointment" because the concepts overlap.
diagnosticCategories.fixPattern: Add explicit disambiguation rules ("reschedule ≠ cancel") to the workflow.
diagnosticCategories.monitoringSignal: Tickets where the AI takes the wrong action on a request it should understand.

ticketScenarios.subject: File a claim for water damage
ticketScenarios.customerMessage: A pipe burst in my kitchen and there's water damage to the floor and cabinets. I need to file a claim ASAP. Policy #INS-441298.
ticketScenarios.aiResponse: I'm sorry to hear about the water damage. I've started a claim under your policy #INS-441298 for general property damage. Your deductible is $1,000 and your coverage limit is $50,000. A claims adjuster will contact you within 5-7 business days. In the meantime, please take photos of the damage and keep all receipts for temporary repairs.
ticketScenarios.idealResponse: I'm so sorry about the pipe burst -- that must be stressful. I've filed an emergency water damage claim under policy #INS-441298. Because water damage is time-sensitive, I've flagged this for our rapid response team -- an adjuster will contact you within 24 hours, not the standard 5-7 days. Your water damage coverage has a $500 deductible (lower than general property) with a $75,000 limit. The prompt didn't include logic to differentiate between damage types and their corresponding claim categories.
ticketScenarios.fixDescription: Add conditional logic to the claims workflow: when damage type involves water/flood/pipe, route to the water damage category (lower deductible, emergency adjuster timeline, mitigation vendor options). Add guardrails to always match the damage type to the correct claim category.

post.description: A fast-paced game that puts you in the support hot seat: triage tickets faster than they pile up. Through the API: a seeded deal of a level's tickets with the answers, scored with the game rules. The web tool is a game. The API deals a seeded set of its tickets, with each step and the right answer, and scores a run with the game rules; it does not play in real time. Stars for a resolved ticket: 3, +1 with no wrong choices, +1 with more than half the timer left, doubled for VIP tickets, then times the combo multiplier on level 5 (1.5x from 2 clean resolves in a row, 2x from 4, 3x from 6). Escalating gives 1 star; an expired ticket costs 1. automationRate is resolved tickets as a share of finished ones; accuracy is right choices as a share of all choices. The rank is for this level on its own (the game keeps a running total across levels). Text in the result is the game copy, with dashes rendered as colons. The game has no URL parameters, so open_in_browser opens the title screen.
